slides.title: Why SLAM
slides.body:
**SLAM** (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping): a robot moving through an unknown environment must simultaneously:

1. Build a map of the environment.
2. Localize itself within the map.

These are coupled. To map, you need to know where you are. To localize, you need a map. SLAM solves both jointly.

**Why it's hard**:

- Sensor noise compounds over time → accumulating drift.
- Loop closure: when revisiting a previous location, the map should be self-consistent. Detecting + correcting this is non-trivial.
- Real-time constraints: robots can't wait minutes for map updates.
- Sensor heterogeneity: cameras, LIDAR, IMU, depth — each with different failure modes + scales.

**Where SLAM matters**: autonomous vehicles (HD-map building + localization), service robots (warehouses, delivery), AR/VR (room reconstruction), drones (search + rescue, mapping).

slides.title: EKF-SLAM (the classical approach)
slides.body:
Treat the robot pose AND all landmarks as a joint state vector. Apply EKF.

**State**: `[robot pose, landmark_1, landmark_2, ..., landmark_N]`. Dimension grows with the number of landmarks.

**Predict**: robot pose updates via motion model; landmarks stay fixed.

**Update**: when sensor sees a landmark, EKF correlates it with stored landmarks; updates joint state.

**Strengths**:

- Conceptually clean.
- Correct under linear-Gaussian assumptions.

**Limits**:

- Quadratic complexity in landmarks: full covariance update is `O(N²)`. Doesn't scale beyond ~hundreds of landmarks.
- Linearization errors accumulate.
- Hard to handle data-association ambiguity (which observed landmark corresponds to which stored one?).

EKF-SLAM was the standard from ~1990 to ~2010. Modern SLAM uses optimization-based + factor-graph methods.

question.question: Why does EKF-SLAM scale poorly with the number of landmarks?
options: The covariance matrix is dense — every landmark is correlated with every other landmark through the joint Bayesian update. Updating this O(N²) matrix at every step is the bottleneck. Modern methods exploit the SPARSITY of the underlying graph (most landmark pairs aren't directly correlated), giving O(N log N) or O(N) updates
question.explanation: The dense covariance matrix is the bottleneck. Modern SLAM exploits sparsity: factor-graph formulations recognize that the underlying problem is sparse, and use sparse linear solvers (Cholesky, QR) for efficient updates.

slides.title: Factor graphs + nonlinear optimization
slides.body:
Modern SLAM (~2010 onwards): formulate as a **factor graph** + solve via nonlinear least squares.

**Factor graph**: bipartite graph with **variables** (poses, landmarks) and **factors** (constraints from measurements). Each factor expresses how likely a measurement is given the variables it connects.

**Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate**: find variable values that minimize the sum of squared residuals across all factors.

`X̂ = argmin_X Σᵢ ||r_i(X)||²_{Σᵢ}`

This is nonlinear least squares; solved via Levenberg-Marquardt or Gauss-Newton.

**Why factor graphs win**:

- **Sparse**: factor graphs are usually very sparse (each measurement constrains a few variables). Sparse Cholesky/QR exploits this.
- **Modular**: adding a new sensor = adding new factors. Adding a new variable = adding a new node.
- **Loop closure**: incorporated as new factors connecting old + recent poses.
- **Real-time**: incremental solvers (iSAM, iSAM2) re-solve only the affected part of the graph.

**Tooling**: GTSAM (Gaussian Belief Networks; Frank Dellaert at Georgia Tech), Ceres Solver (Google), g2o. All production-grade.

slides.title: Loop closure
slides.body:
**Loop closure**: the robot recognizes it has returned to a previously-visited location. Without loop closure, SLAM drift accumulates and the map becomes inconsistent (the same place appears as two separate locations).

**Detection**:

- **Visual loop closure**: compare current image features to a database of past images. Bag-of-words (BoW), VLAD, NetVLAD. Modern: deep-learning visual descriptors (DELF, SuperPoint).
- **LIDAR loop closure**: scan-context, LiDAR-Iris, ICP-based methods.

**Verification**: detected loops can be wrong (perceptual aliasing — two different places look similar). Geometric verification (RANSAC) confirms the match.

**Correction**: the loop adds a factor connecting current pose to the previously-visited pose. Re-solving the optimization redistributes the accumulated error across the entire trajectory.

**Failure modes**:

- **Missed loops**: drift unbounded. Mapping degrades over long trajectories.
- **False loops**: catastrophic. Optimizer corrupts the entire map.

Production SLAM has aggressive loop-closure detection + multiple verification stages to balance these.

question.question: Why is loop closure essential for long-trajectory SLAM?
options: It's not, you can SLAM without it

Without loop closure, drift accumulates monotonically — every step adds estimation error that never gets corrected. After hours of operation, the map is a tangled spaghetti with the same physical place appearing as multiple separate locations. Loop closure is the global consistency mechanism that anchors the trajectory back to known points
question.explanation: Drift is the central problem in SLAM. All sensors have noise; integration accumulates error; without external corrections, the map degrades. Loop closure provides the corrections by anchoring the trajectory to itself when revisits occur.

slides.title: Modern SLAM systems
slides.body:
**ORB-SLAM3**: feature-based visual SLAM. Stereo, monocular, RGB-D supported. Used in research + some production. Open-source.

**Cartographer (Google)**: 2D + 3D LIDAR SLAM. Industrial-strength; deployed in commercial robots.

**LIO-SAM, FAST-LIO**: LIDAR-Inertial systems. Modern; very accurate; fast.

**LeGO-LOAM**: LIDAR odometry + mapping with ground segmentation.

**VINS-Fusion**: visual-inertial SLAM. Open source.

**Neural SLAM**: NICE-SLAM, NeRF-SLAM, Gaussian-Splatting SLAM. Use neural representations for the map. Active research area; deployment-readiness mixed.

**Foundation models for SLAM**: emerging research applying vision foundation models (DINOv2, CLIP-style) to provide robust descriptors for loop closure + multimodal scene understanding.

**Deployment realities**:

- Sensor calibration matters more than algorithm choice for accuracy.
- Time synchronization (microseconds) matters more than feature-detector choice.
- The 'best' SLAM system depends on sensors, environment, computational budget. No universal winner.

The field is mature enough that off-the-shelf SLAM works for many use cases. The frontier: extreme conditions (low-light, fog, rain), long-term operation, multi-agent SLAM, semantic + dynamic SLAM.
